$comment: The executable half of armed-conflict.md beside it. Committed so a run is reproducible and so a reader can see exactly which channels the dashboard was and was not looking at. Run with: python tools/collect/collect.py --run data/osint/briefs/armed-conflict.run.json --out data/osint/<date>-armed-conflict.json

caps.$comment: Looser than the maritime brief's, because the scope is wider rather than because the restraint matters less. A conflict brief that capped at three per channel would take three headlines from a wire service publishing forty relevant ones and call that a picture. Per-platform still binds hardest: one busy platform must not stand in for the world.

termsNote: Each concept is carried in every language the brief covers, because searching in English finds what English publishes and a conflict is reported in the language it happens in. Terms are matched as substrings, which is why the obvious words are absent: 'attack' matches a heart attack and a panic attack, 'killed' matches a road accident, and 'strike' matches industrial action. A term list that over-collects makes the bundle misrepresent what was looked for, which is the one thing a committed brief must not do.
$revision2: Revision 1 carried a bare 'militants', and the danger of a term list this one had already identified in English turned out to apply across languages too. French and Spanish 'militant' means activist: the term's only match in revision 1 was an AFP report of Turkish police raiding gay bars and the homes of 'militants LGBT+', which is a policing operation with no armed-group party and explicitly out of scope. Substrings cannot be conditioned on language, so the fix is collocation. English conflict usage qualifies the word before it -- armed, suspected, militant group -- while the French sense is followed by a cause, so the multi-word forms carry the conflict sense and drop the other. Little is lost: armed group, insurgents, rebels, gunmen and paramilitary already cover an irregular armed party, and 'militants' was the only one of them that was a false friend.

sources.$comment: The same channels the maritime brief verified on 2026-09-13 as serving public content with no credential and no JavaScript. They are reused rather than re-chosen because their public-readability is the property that took work to establish, and because a conflict brief and a maritime one reading the same channels makes the two bundles directly comparable.

State media, read as what it is: a government's account of events, valuable precisely because it states a position and never mistaken for an independent one. The run's main source of Russian-script text.

Kept even when it publishes nothing matching. A source that is listed and produces nothing is a stated gap; a source quietly dropped is an unstated one, and the difference is the whole of why coverage here is measured rather than asserted.
